children.author: bell-cot
children.text:
Limit how many vendors have information about you, even if that's often inconvenient. Especially limit vendors who want too much information. Pay with cash.

Limit how much data any vendor has about you.

Always know who your vendors are. It's far harder to fall for anything that claims to be from FooCo Bank - even if you are distracted and sleep-deprived - if you know that you have no connection to FooCo Bank

For hard-to-avoid vendors who need security questions, keep a paper-only record of per-vendor fabricated answers. Scrape-the-entire-web AI's are a thing now, and your (say) aunt could easily have mentioned your first pet's name on Facebook.

children.author: FinalAngel
drltaidev
children.text: So your answer basically assumes much of your data will get leaked anyway... not a true answer to the question but yeah I do agree. I also agree with all the caution in other replies, but after that still assume your data is leaked and stay suspicious. I don't like answering calls anyway (it's 2026, send me an asynchronous message somehow and let me decide when I reply) so that works well for me.

I'd go the route of not answering calls from numbers I don't know, triaging my emails well and, in general, staying suspicious. Leaked data mostly serves as an attack vector: it gets used to win your trust for social engineering. And to be honest, someone who wants to reach you will find you anyway, through your name on your company's website, social media or some award you once got at school. So be aware, and don't trust anything you haven't confirmed yourself.

Cause even if a Vendor says they removed everything from you, I would trust that all traces are removed. There are logs, backups, analytics etc. and you always leave a footprint on the internet.

children.text: They mail me a bill, and I mail them a check.
How do you not pay your bills online? Do your bring envelopes of money to every business that you work with?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_freeze

I should have said "freeze your credit". But the short of it is, you ask the three credit reporting agencies to refuse to answer questions about your credit. This means that nobody can apply for a loan in your name, because nobody will lend them the money without a credit report. (It also means that you can't take out a new loan, and several other things, including - IIRC - that you can't get a security clearance. To do any of those things, you have to temporarily unfreeze your credit.)

So why did I recommend this? Because almost everyone who is going to use your breached information is going to try to use it to get money, and taking out a loan in your name is the classic way to get it.

Or rather, one of the classic ways. I also should have said, don't do online banking. Don't pay your bills online.
I'm assuming this is a USA centric suggestion. How do you even do this?
Lock down your credit reports.  (I admit that I have not done so.  I should.)

children.author: JulieZhao00
children.text: Using multiple emails, passwords, and phone numbers, also don't use real names input to online websites, i always use my english name not the real name on passport. It helps.

children.author: yencabulator
children.text: Longer term: make companies financially liable.

source.text:
Got another breach email this morning, this travel operator had my passport number and travel history stored. At this point I feel every service we use is going to get dumped eventually.

I consider unique passwords and hardware 2FA as no brainers, they stop credential stuffing, but they don't help when a service leaks your actual identity. There are just so many services that require personal data like your passport number, phone number etc. And I think the fallout will only get worse as agentic workflows and local models become more mainstream and people start giving them more and more personal data.

Assuming every vendor database is basically public eventually, how are you actually limiting the blast radius without turning everyday life into a massive faff?
source.title: Ask HN: Everything will get breached. How do you limit the blast radius?
